Chapter 7: Leadership as Stewardship, Not Control
As the studio found its footing and started to mature, something interesting happened with leadership. In those early days, the leaders were right in the thick of things—solving tricky problems, making quick calls, and setting the pace for everyone else. But as the team got bigger and the projects grew more complex, it became obvious that this hands-on approach just wouldn’t work anymore. So the big question became, what does it really mean to lead when you’re surrounded by creative minds?
For a lot of people, leadership is all about control—making sure everything sticks to the plan. But in a place where the best ideas can come out of nowhere, trying to control everything can actually hold you back. The real job of a leader, it turned out, wasn’t to have all the answers, but to set up the kind of environment where everyone else could do their best work.
There was a project once that really put this to the test. Things were stuck, the director was struggling, and the team was frustrated. It was tempting for a leader to swoop in and take charge—maybe even tell everyone exactly what to do. But that’s not what happened. Instead, the leader started asking questions. What’s tripping you up? What do you need to get back on track? How can I support you?
That’s when it became clear—one of the most powerful things a leader can do is simply listen. By making room for others to figure things out, you give them ownership. Sometimes, that means letting people wrestle with a problem—or even stumble—so they can learn and grow from it. Other times, it’s about clearing roadblocks, shielding the team from outside distractions, or just giving a little encouragement when things get tough.
I remember one moment especially well—a team was just about ready to throw in the towel, totally worn out and discouraged. The leader didn’t try to push harder or demand more effort. Instead, they recognized how tough things were, admitted they had doubts too, and reminded everyone why their work truly mattered. That honesty changed everything. Suddenly, people felt understood—and found the energy to keep going.
Over time, this way of leading became second nature. Leaders weren’t just managing tasks anymore—they were looking after the culture. Their job was to build trust, to be open about their own challenges, and to stand up for the values that made the studio special. Sure, it wasn’t always easy. Old habits still lingered, and the pressure to deliver results never really faded. But by focusing on stewardship instead of just control, the organization managed to grow and still keep its creative spirit alive.
